question: A 34-year-old man is evaluated in the cl inic due to easy bruising. The patient says that even minor trauma causes a bruise and that he sometimes has spontaneous bruising over his legs. He has also experienced generalized fatigue, poor appetite, and dull pain and stiffness in his lower back and joints at night. The patient has a history of Crohn disease that required a partial bowel resection a year ago; he had no excessive bleeding during the perioperative period. Three months ago, he was treated with oral antibiotics for a perianal fistula. Physical examination shows an abdominal wall hematoma and several large ecchymoses on his lower extremities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's excessive bleeding?

options.text: Autoimmune hepatitis 0 B. Bile acid malabsorption 0 C. Factor VII I deficiency 0 D. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis

explanation.text: Although this patient underwent bowel resection for Crohn disease, his persistent fatigue, poor appetite, and joinUback pain (likely representing !BO-associated arthritis) are highly suggestive of recurrenUrefractory disease, which frequently occurs despite operative management. Crohn disease causes transmural inflammation of the bowel wall that most frequently affects the terminal ileum. Bile acids, necessary for the absorption of fat, are normally reabsorbed in the terminal ileum, recycled in the liver, and then reused in the absorptive process (ie, enterohepatic circulation). Patients with extensive terminal ileum inflammation or a history of ileal resection can lose excessive amounts of bile acids in the feces. This causes fat malabsorption, which may lead to deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Vitamin K is a cofactor for several carboxylase enzymes necessary for the activation of coagulation factors 11 , VI I, IX, and X. Coagulation disorders such as vitamin K deficiency typically result in easy bruising, bleeding in deep tissues and joints (eg, muscular hematomas, hemarthrosis) after minor trauma, and prolonged bleeding after surgery.

(Choice A) Because the liver produces most coagulation factors, including vitamin K- dependent factors, autoimmune hepatitis may present with coagulopathy. However, patients with severe coagulopathy would be expected to have other signs of acute liver failure (eg, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites). Furthermore, autoimmune hepatitis is more common in women than men and is more often associated with ulcerative colitis than Crohn disease.

(Choice C) Factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A) is an X-linked recessive coagulation disorder that tends to present in infancy or early childhood. Typical features include easy bruising, hemarthrosis, and prolonged bleeding after surgery (eg, tooth extraction).

(Choice D) Leukocytoclastic vasculitis can be associated with antibiotic use (eg, penicillins, cephalosporins) or viral hepatitis infection; patients usually develop nonblanching petechiae or palpable purpura without excessive bleeding.

educational_objective: Crohn disease with ileal resection or extensive ileal involvement can cause bile acid malabsorption, which may lead to impaired absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Vitamin K deficiency can result in impaired coagulation with easy bruising, large hematoma formation in deep tissues and joints, and prolonged bleeding after surgery.
